# Same-gradient-method comparison: Checkerboard FD vs MITC4 FD

Same `12x8` flat plate, left-edge clamp, nine z-forces, 99 observation nodes,
same central-FD step (`1e-6`), same L-BFGS settings, same target policy.

## Own target (each model reproduces the target generated by its own `f_true`)

| method | iterations | work | total time | target error | free DOF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Checkerboard + FD | 12 | 438 linear solves | 2.08 s | 0.0066% | 297 |
| MITC4 + FD | 17 | 533 forward analyses | 11.85 s | 0.0026% | 594 |

- Total-time ratio: about **5.7x** in favor of Checkerboard.
- Work units are different (linear solves vs full forward analyses); the
  comparison is implementation-level.
- MITC4 rebuilds the model for every FD analysis; a MITC4 adjoint would reduce
  its work units.

## Same target (Checkerboard-generated target)

| method | iterations | work | total time | target error | free DOF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Checkerboard + FD | 12 | 438 linear solves | 2.08 s | 0.0066% | 297 |
| MITC4 + FD | 14 | 514 forward analyses | 10.93 s | 0.555% | 594 |

The MITC4 error is larger because the target is generated by the Checkerboard
model; this is a model difference, not an FD difference.  The cost comparison
is still about `5.2x`.

## What this fills

The previous three-layer table compared Checkerboard **adjoint** with MITC4
**FD**.  This file adds the missing same-gradient-method comparison:
Checkerboard **FD** vs MITC4 **FD**.

It also corrects an earlier mesh mismatch: the old MITC4 row used a `12x12`
mesh (`858` DOF), while the Checkerboard case is `12x8` (`594` MITC4 DOF).
